title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
description: 1271-1275. Escort the young Marco Polo, his father Niccolo, and their trade caravan across the deserts and mountain passes of Central Asia to the court of Kublai Khan. Bandit raiders and harsh terrain threaten the route; the caravan's pack animals must survive. Victory requires bringing Marco alive to the Khan's summer palace at Shangdu.

issues_found: Kublai Khan himself is absent as a unit or character: the destination at Shangdu is only GAIA scenery (a CASTLE, TOWN_CENTER and two GUARD_TOWERs), so the man whose court the journey was undertaken to reach never appears.
Maffeo Polo, Niccolo's brother and the third member of the party on the 1271 departure, is entirely missing; the text speaks only of father and son.

The 'pack camels' are CAMEL_RIDER units — armed light cavalry standing in for baggage animals — when the engine offers TRADE_CART/trade cargo units that would far better represent a merchant caravan's goods.

Escort composition of 2 KNIGHTs, 3 MAN_AT_ARMS and 3 CROSSBOWMEN gives the Polos a Latin-European men-at-arms retinue; the Venetians travelled as merchants under Mongol safe-conduct (the Khan's golden tablet), not with heavy Western cavalry.

Attributing the ambush to 'Khaidu's horsemen' conflates Kaidu's dynastic war against Kublai with anonymous desert banditry; Polo's own account of the route dangers (Karaunas brigands, the Gobi crossing) is not what is depicted.
The party's actual hardships — Marco's long illness in Badakhshan, the year lost in the Pamirs and Gobi — are reduced to a single scripted PATROL ambush of 10 raiders.
